Fused deposition modeling (FDM) was used to fabricate polymer matrix composite components, with improvements made to reduce porosity and increase mechanical properties.
Binder jet printing was used to fabricate ceramic matrix composite components, with optimization of powder composition and addition of chopped SiC fibers.
Prototype components like inlet guide vanes, compressor blades, and acoustic liners were fabricated and tested in relevant operating conditions.
Engine system analysis showed the non-metallic engine design could reduce engine weight by 15% and aircraft fuel burn by 4.9%, with an 8.3% decrease in NOx emissions.
The technology readiness level (TRL) of the fused deposition modeling process for polymers was assessed at TRL 4, while the binder jet process for ceramics was at TRL 3.
Key challenges included reducing porosity in polymers, optimizing binder jet infiltration for ceramics, and addressing dimensional tolerances and in-situ damage characterization.
Chopped fiber reinforcement increased the modulus of high-temperature polymers by 40% in the FDM process.
Optimizing the powder composition and size distribution was critical for improving packing and infiltration in the binder jet ceramic composites.
Up to 35 vol% chopped SiC fibers were added to the binder jet powder bed to fabricate the first CMC turbine engine components by additive manufacturing.
Next steps include further optimizing constituent materials, exploring alternate densification approaches, investigating fiber coatings, and reducing porosity in polymers.
Engine system modeling tools like NPSS and FLOPS were used to quantify the potential benefits of the non-metallic engine design.
Ultem 1000 was used as the high-temperature polymer matrix material in the FDM process for composite components.
SiC powders with median grain sizes ranging from 9 to 53 microns were evaluated for the binder jet ceramic composites.
SMP-10 polycarbosilane and phenolic resins were used as infiltrants for the binder jet ceramic matrix composites.
Si-TUFF SiC fibers with 7 micron mean diameter and 65-70 micron mean length were used as the reinforcement in the CMCs.
